cards.title: The serpent in the Garden of Eden

source.name: Geneva Bible 1599
source.citation: Genesis 3:1–15 (Geneva 1599): the serpent deceives Eve, bringing sin and death into the world and earning God's curse.

cards.summary_basic: In Genesis, the serpent (understood by Shakespeare's readers as Satan in disguise) tempts Eve in the Garden of Eden, bringing sin, death, and exile from paradise. When the Ghost reveals that 'the serpent that did sting thy father's life / now wears his crown,' the murder in the orchard is cast in Eden's terms: Claudius is the satanic intruder, and the dead king an Adam dispossessed of his garden.
cards.detail_scholar: The Geneva Bible's marginal note glosses the serpent as the instrument of 'Satan.' Shakespeare reinforces the parallel by framing the murder in an 'orchard' (an enclosed garden) and by the Ghost's language of a paradise corrupted from within. The serpent-as-betrayer was among the most instantly legible biblical images for an Elizabethan audience.

cards.title: The Sixth Commandment and self-slaughter

source.name: Geneva Bible 1599
source.citation: Exodus 20:13 (Geneva 1599): 'Thou shalt not kill.' Compare Deuteronomy 5:17.

cards.summary_basic: The commandment 'Thou shalt not kill' (the sixth in the Protestant numbering used in Shakespeare's England; the fifth in Catholic and Lutheran tradition) was understood in Elizabethan theology to forbid suicide as well as murder — killing oneself was 'self-slaughter,' a sin against God, who alone gives and takes life. The Church refused full Christian burial to suicides. This is why Hamlet says God 'fix'd / his canon 'gainst self-slaughter,' and why Ophelia's drowning is so anxiously debated in Act 5.
cards.detail_scholar: Here 'canon' means a divine law or decree (not a cannon). The doctrine that suicide damns the soul and forfeits consecrated burial gives weight to Hamlet's wish that his flesh would simply 'melt' — he is barred from hastening it. The theme returns at the graveside, where the priest grants Ophelia only 'maimed rites.'

cards.title: Cain and Abel: the first murder

source.name: Geneva Bible 1599
source.citation: Genesis 4:1–16 (Geneva 1599): Cain kills his brother Abel; God sets a curse and a mark upon him.

cards.summary_basic: In Genesis, Cain murders his brother Abel out of envy — the first murder in the Bible, and a killing of brother by brother. Claudius (who murdered his brother, Hamlet's father) names his own crime through this story: 'It hath the primal eldest curse upon't, / A brother's murder.' In the graveyard the gravedigger jokes that a thrown skull is like 'Cain's jaw-bone, that did the first murder.'
cards.detail_scholar: The Bible does not say what weapon Cain used; the 'jawbone' is a medieval legend (probably borrowed from Samson's jawbone in Judges 15). The Cain story makes Claudius's fratricide resonate as the archetypal, God-cursed sin.

cards.title: Jephthah's daughter

source.name: Geneva Bible 1599
source.citation: Judges 11:30–40 (Geneva 1599): Jephthah vows to sacrifice the first thing that greets him on return, and it is his only daughter.

cards.summary_basic: Jephthah, a judge of Israel, rashly vowed to God that if he won his battle he would sacrifice whatever first came out of his house to meet him — and it was his beloved only daughter. Hamlet taunts Polonius by calling him 'Jephthah, judge of Israel': a father whose folly will destroy his own daughter. It is a chilling forecast of what happens to Ophelia.

cards.title: The fall of a sparrow

source.name: Geneva Bible 1599
source.citation: Matthew 10:29 (Geneva 1599): 'Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing, and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father?'

cards.summary_basic: Jesus tells his disciples that not even a sparrow — the cheapest of birds — falls to the ground without God's knowledge and will. Facing the duel he senses may kill him, Hamlet reaches a calm: 'we defy augury: there's a special providence in the fall of a sparrow.' He stops trying to read omens and accepts that the timing of death is in God's hands — 'the readiness is all.'
cards.detail_scholar: This is the play's clearest statement of Christian providence, and a turn away from the pagan revenge-tragedy machinery of omens and ghosts toward acceptance.

cards.title: Pilate washing his hands

source.name: Geneva Bible 1599
source.citation: Matthew 27:24 (Geneva 1599): Pilate 'tooke water, and washed his handes before the multitude, saying, I am innocent of the blood of this just man.'

cards.summary_basic: When the crowd bayed for Jesus's death, the Roman governor Pontius Pilate publicly washed his hands to disown responsibility for the killing he was about to allow. At his deposition Richard flings the gesture back at the lords who claim clean hands in his fall: 'Though some of you, with Pilate, wash your hands, / Showing an outward pity; yet you Pilates / Have here deliver'd me to my sour cross' (4.1) — casting himself as a Christ betrayed and condemned.
cards.detail_scholar: Richard repeatedly likens his fall to Christ's Passion: he speaks of being sold by 'Judases' (the favourites, and Northumberland), of finding 'in twelve thousand none' faithful, and here of his 'sour cross.' The Pilate allusion turns the deposing lords into participants in a sacrilege — washing the hands cannot wash away the guilt of delivering up an anointed king. The futility of hand-washing as a cleansing of blood-guilt returns powerfully in Macbeth.

cards.title: The Prodigal Son

source.name: Geneva Bible 1599
source.citation: Luke 15:11-32 (Geneva 1599); the husks the prodigal envies the swine at Luke 15:16.

cards.summary_basic: Jesus's parable of a younger son who demands his inheritance early, squanders it abroad in 'riotous living,' is reduced to feeding pigs and longing to eat their husks, then returns home in shame — where his father joyfully forgives him and kills the fatted calf to feast. The arc shadows Prince Hal, who seems to waste his youth among tavern thieves before returning to his royal father; Falstaff jokes that his ragged recruits look like 'prodigals lately come from swine-keeping, from eating draff and husks' (4.2).
cards.detail_scholar: Hal's soliloquy 'I know you all' (1.2) recasts his riot as a deliberate, temporary fall he will redeem — a planned prodigal's return staged for maximum effect. The parable was a stock subject of the painted cloths that hung in taverns and inns (Falstaff alludes to such hangings), making it doubly apt for the Eastcheap world. Shakespeare develops the prodigal motif further in Henry IV Part 2 and the rejection of Falstaff.

cards.title: Dives and Lazarus

source.name: Geneva Bible 1599
source.citation: Luke 16:19-31 (Geneva 1599); the rich man in purple and the beggar Lazarus whose sores the dogs licked.

cards.summary_basic: Jesus's parable of a rich man (traditionally called Dives, Latin for 'rich,' clothed in purple and feasting every day) and a starving beggar, Lazarus, covered in sores that dogs licked at the rich man's gate. Both die: Lazarus is carried to Abraham's bosom, the rich man to torment in hell-fire. Falstaff invokes both figures — his tattered conscripts are 'as ragged as Lazarus in the painted cloth, where the glutton's dogs licked his sores' (4.2), and he mocks Bardolph's fiery-red face as a reminder of 'Dives that lived in purple; for there he is in his robes, burning, burning' (3.3).
cards.detail_scholar: Like the Prodigal Son, the story was a common subject of cheap 'painted cloth' wall-hangings, which Falstaff repeatedly references; the joke assumes the audience can picture the standard image. Bardolph's flaming complexion as a memento mori of hell-fire is one of the play's running gags. 'Dives' is not a name in the Geneva text but the long-standing nickname for the rich man.

cards.title: The Queen of Sheba (Saba)

source.name: Geneva Bible 1599
source.citation: 1 Kings 10:1–13 (Geneva 1599); compare 2 Chronicles 9:1–12 — the Queen of Sheba comes to test Solomon's wisdom with hard questions.

cards.summary_basic: In the Bible, the Queen of Sheba (called 'Saba' in older spelling), hearing of King Solomon's fame, travels to Jerusalem to test his wisdom with hard questions and is left breathless by his understanding. In Cranmer's christening prophecy the infant Elizabeth is promised even greater gifts: 'Saba was never / More covetous of wisdom and fair virtue / Than this pure soul shall be' (5.5) — the Old Testament byword for a wisdom-seeking monarch is named only to be surpassed.
cards.detail_scholar: 'Saba' follows the older Vulgate spelling of Sheba. The Geneva account (1 Kings 10) stresses that the queen came 'to proue him with hard questions' and that Solomon resolved them all — the very emblem of royal wisdom the prophecy claims, and then outbids, for Elizabeth. The allusion belongs to the panegyric mode of the christening scene, which ranks the newborn princess above the most celebrated wisdom-seeker of scripture.

cards.title: The fall of the angels (Lucifer's pride)

source.name: Geneva Bible 1599
source.citation: Isaiah 14:12 (Geneva 1599): 'How art thou fallen from heauen, O Lucifer, sonne of the morning!'; compare Luke 10:18 and Revelation 12:7–9 — the rebel angels cast out of heaven.

cards.summary_basic: Christian tradition held that Lucifer and the rebel angels were cast out of heaven for the sin of pride and ambition — exalting themselves against God. The fallen Cardinal Wolsey turns this lesson on himself when he counsels his servant Cromwell: 'Cromwell, I charge thee, fling away ambition: / By that sin fell the angels' (3.2). His political ruin becomes a homily on overreaching — the same sin that toppled the brightest of the angels.
cards.detail_scholar: The name 'Lucifer' ('light-bearer,' the morning star) comes from Isaiah 14:12, a taunt addressed to the king of Babylon that Christian readers applied to Satan's fall through pride — linked to Luke 10:18 ('I saw Satan fall like lightning') and the war in heaven of Revelation 12. Wolsey's couplet makes his fall moral and almost cosmic: the de casibus pattern given its ultimate theological form. Ambition figured as a Luciferian fall recurs across Shakespeare (Macbeth's 'vaulting ambition,' the overreachers of the histories).

cards.title: Samson and Delilah (and Solomon's wives)

source.name: Geneva Bible 1599
source.citation: Judges 16:4-21 (Geneva 1599): Samson, strongest of the Israelite judges, loves Delilah, who coaxes from him the secret of his strength — his unshorn hair — and betrays him to the Philistines, who shear and blind him. Compare 1 Kings 11:1-4: Solomon's many foreign wives turn his heart from God. In Love's Labour's Lost 1.2 Armado consoles himself that strong Samson and wise Solomon were also conquered by love.

cards.summary_basic: Samson, the strongest of the biblical judges, was undone by his love for Delilah, who wheedled out the secret of his strength — his uncut hair — and handed him over to his enemies, who blinded him. With Solomon, the wisest king, whose foreign wives led him into idolatry, he was a stock example of the great man toppled by love. The love-struck Armado cites both to excuse his own folly.
cards.detail_scholar: The pairing belongs to a popular medieval and Renaissance topos, the 'Power of Women,' in which even the strongest (Samson), the wisest (Solomon), and the greatest were brought low by desire. In 1.2 the infatuated Armado asks 'what great men have been in love?' and takes comfort that Samson — 'a man of good carriage,' who carried off the town gates of Gaza (Judges 16:3) — and Solomon succumbed too. Samson's story runs through Judges 13-16; Solomon's foreign wives are in 1 Kings 11. The same examples recur wherever Shakespeare's lovers plead that love conquers even the mightiest.

cards.title: St Paul's Ephesus: magic and marriage

source.name: Geneva Bible 1599
source.citation: Acts 19 (Geneva 1599): St Paul at Ephesus — the seven sons of Sceva and the Jewish exorcists, the burning of the books of 'curious arts' (magic), and the riot of the silversmiths of 'Diana of the Ephesians.' Compare Ephesians 5:22-33: the household code on wives and husbands. Shakespeare's move of the action to Ephesus evokes both a city proverbial for sorcery and the scene of Paul's teaching on marriage.

cards.summary_basic: Shakespeare shifts the action from Plautus's Epidamnus to Ephesus — a city that for Bible-reading Elizabethans meant two things at once. In Acts 19 Ephesus is full of exorcists and magicians whose spell-books are burned at St Paul's preaching; and Paul's Epistle to the Ephesians gives the famous rule that wives should submit to their husbands and husbands love their wives. Both lie behind the play's talk of witchcraft and its marriage quarrels.
cards.detail_scholar: The setting is pointed. The bewildered Syracusans keep blaming the city's reputation for sorcery — 'they say this town is full of cozenage, / As nimble jugglers that deceive the eye... soul-killing witches that deform the body,' 'Lapland sorcerers,' the fear of being 'transform'd' — which echoes the Ephesus of Acts 19, with its exorcists, burned books of magic, and cult of Diana. Meanwhile Luciana's lecture to Adriana on a wife's duty, and Adriana's reply, play against Ephesians 5:22-33 ('Wives, submit yourselves unto your husbands... husbands, love your wives'). The closing scene in a priory, the Abbess's almost sacramental language, and the long-lost family reborn give the Roman farce an unexpectedly redemptive, Pauline frame.

cards.title: Jacob and Laban's sheep

source.name: Geneva Bible 1599
source.citation: Genesis 30:25-43 (Geneva 1599): serving his uncle Laban, Jacob takes as his wages the speckled and spotted of the flock, and increases them by setting peeled rods before the ewes as they breed; compare Genesis 29-31 for the wider story of Jacob and Laban.

cards.summary_basic: In Genesis, Jacob agrees to work for his uncle Laban for wages of all the speckled and spotted lambs born to the flock, then makes the ewes bear more of them by a trick with peeled rods. Shylock retells this in 1.3 to argue that profit shrewdly won is a blessing from God: 'This was a way to thrive, and he was blest; / And thrift is blessing, if men steal it not.' Antonio rejects the analogy — Jacob's increase was 'sway'd and fashion'd by the hand of heaven,' not gained, like interest, by making money breed money.
cards.detail_scholar: The deal and the rods are at Genesis 30:25-43; the 'eanlings' (newborn lambs) that fall 'streak'd and pied' are Jacob's hire. Shylock uses Hebrew scripture to defend lending at interest (see usury-and-the-bond); Antonio counters that a venture under God's providence is not the same as usury. The exchange stages Jew and Christian each laying claim to the Old Testament — a recurring move in a play where both sides quote the same God against each other.

cards.title: 'With what measure ye mete': the title from the Sermon on the Mount

source.name: Geneva Bible 1599
source.citation: Matthew 7:1-2 (Geneva 1599): 'Judge not, that ye be not judged. For with what judgement ye judge, ye shall be judged; and with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again.' Compare the Duke's sentence 'measure still for measure' (5.1) and the law of retaliation, 'eye for eye,' at Exodus 21:23-25.

cards.summary_basic: The play's title comes from Jesus's warning in the Sermon on the Mount: judge others and you invite the same judgement, for the standard ('measure') you apply will be applied to you. The Duke pronounces 'measure still for measure' (5.1) when he turns Angelo's own death-sentence back upon him. The play tests whether human justice can ever live up to the divine standard of mercy that Jesus urges — or whether, applied strictly, 'measure for measure' would damn every judge.
cards.detail_scholar: The same chapter (Matthew 7:3-5) tells the judge to 'first cast out the beam out of thine own eye' before the mote in his brother's — precisely Angelo's failing as he condemns Claudio for the very sin he then commits. 'Measure for measure' also echoes the lex talionis ('an eye for an eye') of Exodus and Leviticus, which the Sermon on the Mount revises toward mercy ('resist not evil'). Isabella's plea — 'How would you be / If He, which is the top of judgement, should / But judge you as you are?' (2.2) — is the Sermon's lesson turned on Angelo, and looks ahead to Portia's 'in the course of justice none of us / Should see salvation.'
